idiom_name: Express middleware that denies unless a grant is found; fail-closed error path
implementation_notes: Node ships no authorization layer, so the rule is middleware discipline: one guard mounted before the routes (`app.use` executes in registration order, as the Express guide documents) that resolves the request to a grant and otherwise ends the cycle with 401/403, plus handlers that treat a missing `req.user` or `req.grant` as a denial. The characteristic fail-open trap is the error path: an `await` inside the guard that rejects must end in a denial, not in `next()`, so `try { await check(); next(); } catch { next(); }` converts a broken policy lookup into open access. Keep the decision a single function (so unknown inputs can be tested) and make the public surface explicit - a route that needs no grant should be a named exception rather than a route that never got the middleware.
pitfalls: `catch { next(); }` is the fail-open path: an unreachable policy service or a thrown error must deny (403/503), never continue; the same applies to a decision helper that returns true when the lookup throws.

Mount order: a guard registered after the routes never runs for them, and a router mounted later inserts its routes after the guard only if the guard sits on the app - keep the guard first and re-verify when routers are added.

`req.user` set by an optional authenticator is not authorization: a handler that tests `if (req.user)` and otherwise proceeds, or a guard that permits when the user is absent 'because it is a public page', inverts the default.

Policy lookups keyed on a plain object inherit `Object.prototype` members: `grants[action]` is truthy for `constructor` or `toString`, so use a `Map`, `Object.create(null)` or `hasOwn` in the decision.

Express 5 turns a rejected promise from middleware into `next(err)`; without an error handler the default handler returns 500 (safe), but an error handler that renders a page and continues processing can restore the request - guard error handling must terminate.
